A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching estimator and main theorems. Text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices are readable, including Appendices A–F in v2 and A–G in v3.

before.justification: Section 4 and Appendix F report original simulations comparing estimators under adversarial disturbances, different input distributions, activation functions, and memory lengths.

after.justification: v3 retains original simulation results and reports additional power-grid experiments and observation-dimension sensitivity results in Section 4.2 and Appendices F–G.

M1.justification: The finite-memory basis representation and the sum-of-Euclidean-residual-norms estimator in Equation (12) remain unchanged. The power-grid experiment instantiates this estimator with application-specific features; it introduces no new estimation algorithm.

E1.justification: Section 4.2 and Appendix G add power-grid identification from mechanical power injections to partially observed rotor angles and speeds. This substantially extends the previous random-matrix synthetic coverage to an application domain, evaluated through a discretized, linearized swing-dynamics model.

E2.justification: The evaluated comparator sets remain least-squares versus ℓ2, and ℓ1 versus ℓ2 versus ℓ∞. The new grid experiment and dimension study reuse these respective sets. Removing the Ziemann row from the conceptual literature table does not remove an experimentally evaluated baseline.

E3.justification: The new dimension study evaluates r=5 and r=100 alongside the retained r=10 experiments. The grid experiment introduces linearization, a sampling interval of 0.001, and an input-dependent attack construction. Existing synthetic-data splits, kernel settings, and error metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix F adds Figure 5, testing how observation dimension affects ℓ1, ℓ2, and ℓ∞ estimation under both activation functions. The earlier memory-length, contraction-factor, and activation-boundedness analyses remain, with v2 Figure 3 corresponding to v3 Figure 4.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 95% confidence intervals based on standard errors from 10 experiments with randomized system matrices and disturbances. v3 introduces no stated change in repeat counts, seeds, confidence levels, or uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Figures 3 and 5 add grid results favoring ℓ2 over least-squares and dimension-dependent errors showing deterioration for all three norm estimators. Existing synthetic curves also change: for example, uniform-input least-squares error at T=300 is approximately 90 in v2 Figure 3a versus 80 in v3 Figure 4a under the retained reported settings. Broad estimator rankings remain similar.

T1.justification: Assumption 2.6 changes the conditioning filtration from initial state, inputs, and past disturbances to state history alone. Assumption 2.8 removes the explicit Bernoulli-independence-from-filtration clause. Theorem 3.1 now explicitly covers any matrix satisfying the bounded approximation condition. Main bound formulas and proofs in Appendices B–E otherwise remain essentially unchanged; Appendix G adds the grid-model derivation.

C1.justification: The central finite-memory identification and matching O(ρ^τ)/Ω(ρ^τ) claims remain. The new Impact Statement adds an explicit priority claim that this is the first work establishing optimal input-output estimation bounds under probabilistic adversarial attacks.

C2.justification: v3 acknowledges that increasing ℓ2 error with observation dimension in Figure 5 is not perfectly consistent with its dimension-independent interpretation, although ℓ2 remains least affected. It also clarifies that the approximating matrix need not be unique and expands practical input motivations. Existing memory-length tradeoffs and lower-bound limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds grid parameter ranges, discretization, regressor construction, and an explicit attack formula. Appendix F specifies matrix dimensions for the new observation study. Existing hardware, MOSEK use, polynomial-kernel settings, regularization selection, and data-splitting details are retained.

R1.justification: v3 adds Bakshi et al. (2023), Stone (1948), Park and Sandberg (1991), and Kumar and Varaiya (2016). The introduction and Appendix A more explicitly distinguish restricted-history adversaries from the paper's sparse-attack setting and connect that setting to Kim and Lavaei's work. Most related-work discussion remains.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites explain probabilistic attacks, approximation tolerance, and practical inputs. Section 4 gains synthetic and power-system subsections, and an Impact Statement and Appendix G are added. The existing section order and most theoretical prose remain intact.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column conference formatting. Figure 1's panels are stacked, explanatory boxes are introduced, and Table 1 loses two comparison columns and one row. Existing plots are redrawn, and Figures 3 and 5 and Table 2 are added; the old appendix Figure 3 becomes Figure 4.

improvement.justification: v3 clarifies the approximation target and adds an informative dimension-sensitivity study with an explicit empirical caveat. However, its new grid validation has unresolved reproducibility problems: Appendix G's attack formula is always nonnegative despite the claimed sign-changing attacks, and grid size and input-generation settings are unspecified. These issues limit confidence in an important part of the added evidence, preventing a reliable net quality judgment.
